newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Bid to boost economy backfires for Nigerian naira.
newsitem.headline: Bid to boost economy backfires for Nigerian naira.

text.p: Pumping too much money into circulation in an attempt to stimulate the Nigerian economy has forced the authorities to devalue the naira ahead of crucial local council elections at the weekend.
The central bank said from Thursday the naira would exchange at the weekly auction of foreign currency at 85 instead of 80 to the dollar, a 5.88 percent devaluation.

"It is only nine weeks into fiscal 1997 and yet Nigeria appears to have fallen already on harder economic times," said Business News, a publication of the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry in its latest edition on Thursday.

The devaluation, the first in more than two years and after the authorities thought the exchange rate had stabilised, comes before elections on Saturday aimed at democratising the third and lowest tier of Nigeria's government.

Official meetings in the capital Abuja have been followed by statements that the election will be trouble-free. If they succeed the military government can uphold them as evidence that it is on course to hand over to an elected president.
But for the business community the devaluation is a more important issue and is a sign that the economy remains fargile.
"This devaluation is a big blow although we saw it coming," said Yomi Adebola, who runs a money exchange shop in Lagos.
The central bank and other business operators blame the devaluation on the ballooning volume of money in circulation.
A senior central bank official said recently that there was 111 billion naira in circulation, most of it outside banks.
The situation seems to have been triggered by government policies included in the 1997 budget released in mid-January.

A tight fiscal policy over the last two years had reasonably stabilised the main facets of the economy, which like most other aspects of life in Nigeria suffered from a 1993 annulment of a presidential election to restore democracy.
The annulment led to Nigeria being shunned by its traditional Western partners and sanctions that have reduced investment flow into the populous African nation.
Recently Ernest Shonekan, former interim leader and chairman of a Vision 2010 group appointed to fashion Nigeria's future, admitted that the sanctions were beginning to bite.
Economists agreed that while the economy had stabilised, growth at just three percent a year was inadequate to make a difference in the lives of ordinary people.
So in January the government announced a budget to reflate the economy, setting a growth target of 5.5 percent.

"The budget created the run on the naira by allowing too much money in circulation and the banks don't know what to do with the money because there are no instruments to invest them in," said banker Samuel Asom.
"There are no easy and tested channels for moving money in a largely urbanised banking sector into the largely rural mineral and agricutural sector that the government wants it," he added.
The result is that money is moving into the stock market and the weekly foreign exchange auction called AFEM (Autonomus Foreign Exchange Market).
Prices of stocks have risen strongly in the last month while demand for foreign exchange at the auctions shot to $94 million last week from the normal weekly level of about $70 million.
Since then economists have warned that if not checked this could cause a crash in the value of the naira.
To check bogus demands, the central bank has called for detailed information on the end-users of the foreign exchange banks had bought at the AFEM over the last month.
But analysts said more radical measures were needed.

"Until government puts in place a package of policies to address the issue of commercial convertibility of the naira it will continue to depreciate," said executive chairman of African Commodity Services Company, Ashikiwe Adione-Egom.
